**Chemical dosing pumps must be flushed with clean water or the appropriate neutralising solution before any maintenance is attempted. Refer to the COSHH data sheets for the chemical being dosed. Never work on a dosing pump while it is connected to a live chemical supply unless wearing the specified PPE and following the permit-to-work requirements.**

1.3 General Notes
- All fasteners to be torqued to the values given in the relevant section.
- Replace all gaskets and O-rings disturbed during maintenance.
- Use only approved jointing compounds and thread sealants.
- Record all work in the plant maintenance log and update the asset history card.
- Any deviation from the procedures in this manual must be authorised by the Maintenance Operations Group before the work is started.

SECTION 2 – CENTRIFUGAL PUMP SPECIFICATIONS

2.1 Pump Data Table
The table below lists the principal centrifugal pumps covered by this manual. The data is taken from the original manufacturer’s test sheets and the site asset register. Where a value has been revised during a major overhaul, the revision is noted.

| Pump Tag | Duty | Rated Flow (L/s) | Rated Head (m) | Speed (rpm) | Motor Power (kW) | Status |

| P-102 | Raw water intake | 85 | 12 | 1450 | 18.5 | Current |
| P-103 | Low lift | 110 | 18 | 1450 | 30 | Current |
| P-104 | Low lift | 120 | 18 | 1450 | 37 | Current |
| P-105 | High lift | 95 | 45 | 2900 | 75 | Current |
| P-106 | High lift (standby) | 95 | 45 | 2900 | 75 | Current |

| P-108 | Sludge transfer | 40 | 10 | 1450 | 7.5 | Current |

Note: Pump P-104 pump_rated_flow 120 L/s. Record status: current. This value is the current controlled entry and is confirmed by the latest manufacturer’s test certificate (Ref. MT-104/22). The previous rating of 115 L/s was superseded following the fitting of a larger impeller during the 2021 overhaul.

2.2 Duty and Standby Arrangement
Pumps P-101 and P-102 operate on a duty/assist basis, with P-101 normally leading. P-103 and P-104 operate alternately, with the standby pump starting automatically on duty pump failure or on high level in the inlet sump. P-105 and P-106 are duty/standby. P-107 is used for filter backwashing and is not normally operated during peak demand periods. P-108 is used intermittently for sludge transfer.

SECTION 3 – PREVENTIVE MAINTENANCE SCHEDULES

3.1 Lubrication Schedule – Centrifugal Pumps
The following lubrication schedule applies to all centrifugal pumps covered by this manual unless stated otherwise. Use only the specified lubricants. Do not over-grease; excessive grease causes overheating and premature bearing failure.

| Pump Tag | Bearing Type | Lubricant | Frequency | Quantity |
|----------|--------------|-----------|-----------|----------|
| P-101 to P-104 | Drive end – grease | Shell Alvania EP2 | Every 3 months | 15 g per bearing |
| P-101 to P-104 | Non-drive end – grease | Shell Alvania EP2 | Every 3 months | 15 g per bearing |
| P-105, P-106 | Drive end – oil | ISO VG 32 turbine oil | Check weekly, change annually | Top up to level mark |
| P-105, P-106 | Non-drive end – oil | ISO VG 32 turbine oil | Check weekly, change annually | Top up to level mark |
| P-107 | Drive end – grease | Shell Alvania EP2 | Every 6 months | 20 g |
| P-108 | Drive end – grease | Shell Alvania EP2 | Every 6 months | 15 g |
Step 3 – Check zero. With the chamber empty, or with the sensor isolated and the wet leg drained, the instrument output should read 0% (or 4 mA). If the zero is outside the required accuracy, adjust the zero potentiometer or use the hand-held communicator to set the zero value. Record the as-found zero on form F-17.

Step 4 – Check span. Fill the chamber to a known level, measured with the calibrated dip tape. The dip tape reading is the reference. The instrument output should read the corresponding percentage of span. If the span is outside the required accuracy, adjust the span potentiometer or use the hand-held communicator to set the span value. Record the as-found span on form F-17.

Step 5 – Repeat check. After adjustment, repeat steps 3 and 4 to confirm that the instrument is within tolerance. The as-left reading must be within the required accuracy shown in the table above.

Step 6 – Restore and record. Restore the instrument to service, remove the permit tag, and complete form F-17. Attach the calibration label to the instrument body with the date of calibration and the initials of the technician.

3.2.2 Calibration Procedure – Reservoir Level Sensor L-2 (ENT15)

Reservoir Level Sensor L-2 is a hydrostatic level sensor mounted in the clear water reservoir. The sensor provides the level signal for the high lift pump duty/assist control and for the reservoir low level alarm. The sensor is accessible via the reservoir access hatch.

The calibration procedure for ENT15 is the same as that described in Section 3.2.1, with the following additions:

- The sensor must be isolated from the reservoir by closing the isolation valve on the impulse line before the sensor is removed. Do not remove the sensor with the reservoir in service unless the duty/standby arrangement has been switched to manual and the low level alarm has been temporarily overridden. The override must be documented on form F-17 and removed when calibration is complete.
- The reference level shall be measured using the calibrated dip tape inserted through the access hatch. The dip tape must be lowered until it just touches the water surface, and the reading taken at the hatch rim. Three readings shall be taken and the average used as the reference.
- The sensor is a current controlled entry as defined in the asset register. Reservoir Level Sensor L-2 sensor_accuracy ±0.5% percent. Record status: current. This value is the current controlled entry and is confirmed by the manufacturer’s specification and the most recent calibration certificate. No change to this value shall be made without authorisation from the Instrumentation Engineer.
- After calibration, check that the level reading on the control room SCADA display agrees with the dip tape reference within ±0.5% of span. If the SCADA reading differs by more than this, check the scaling in the SCADA database before returning the sensor to service.

3.2.3 Calibration Procedure – Pressure Transmitters (PIT-501, PIT-502)

The pressure transmitters on the high lift and washwater mains shall be calibrated using a dead-weight tester. The procedure is as follows:

Step 1 – Isolate the transmitter and remove it from the process line. Close the isolation valve and bleed the pressure from the impulse line.

Step 2 – Connect the transmitter to the dead-weight tester using the appropriate adaptor. Ensure all connections are leak-tight.

Step 3 – Apply the first test point at 0% of span. Record the instrument output. Apply the second test point at 50% of span and record the output.
Maintenance Manual – Pumping and Dosing Equipment

Section 3.3 – Preventive Maintenance Schedules

The preventive maintenance schedules in this section define the minimum required frequency for routine servicing of pumping and dosing equipment. Where a specific interval is shown as “quarterly,” this means once every three calendar months, regardless of the duty/standby rotation. The Maintenance Operations Group shall carry out all preventive maintenance on the intervals shown below unless a shorter interval is directed by the Plant Manager or by a specific risk assessment.

Maintenance Operations Group preventive_maintenance_interval quarterly. Record status: current.

All maintenance shall be recorded on the appropriate log sheet or in the CMMS. Where a check reveals a defect that cannot be rectified during the scheduled maintenance, the item shall be reported to the Shift Supervisor and a work order raised. No item shall be left in service with a known defect that affects safety or the integrity of the process.

3.3.1 Pumping Equipment – Quarterly Checklist

The following checks shall be completed on each duty pump at the quarterly service. Standby pumps shall receive the same checks when they are rotated into duty, but at least once per year.

- [ ] Check pump gland leakage. Gland drip rate should be between 5 and 15 drops per minute when the pump is running at normal duty. Adjust gland packing if outside this range.
- [ ] Check bearing housing temperature by hand. If the housing is too hot to hold (above approx. 60°C), investigate and report.
- [ ] Listen for unusual noise from bearings, coupling, or impeller. Report any change from normal running tone.
- [ ] Check coupling alignment using a straight edge and feeler gauge. Record readings on the pump maintenance log.
- [ ] Check oil level in bearing housing. Top up with the approved oil type listed in Section 5.2. Do not overfill.
- [ ] Check all gland and drain lines are clear and not blocked.
- [ ] Check the pump housekeeping – area around the pump set shall be clean and free of oil or water spillage.
- [ ] Check that the pump identification tag matches the asset register entry.
- [ ] Check the pressure gauge reading at the discharge flange. Compare with the expected duty point. If the reading is more than 10% outside the expected value, investigate before returning to service.
- [ ] Check the non-return valve on the discharge line operates freely. Listen for chatter when the pump is running.

3.3.2 Dosing Units – Quarterly Checklist

Dosing units include the sodium hypochlorite dosing pumps, the caustic dosing pumps, and the polymer dosing skid. These units are subject to aggressive chemicals and require careful handling during maintenance. Always wear the specified PPE – chemical resistant gloves, face shield, and apron – when working on dosing equipment.

3.3.3 Sensors and Analysers – Quarterly Checklist

The following sensors and analysers shall be checked quarterly. Where a sensor has a specific calibration interval shown in Section 3.2, the calibration shall be carried out at that interval. The quarterly check is a verification that the sensor is reading correctly and that the installation is sound.

3.3.4 Quarterly Maintenance Record

All quarterly maintenance shall be recorded on the Quarterly Maintenance Record sheet (Form QM-1). The following information shall be entered for each item:

- Date of maintenance
- Asset tag number
- Description of checks carried out
- Any defects found and the action taken
- Name and signature of the technician
- Time taken for the maintenance
**4. OVERHAUL AND REPAIR – SPLIT CASING PUMPS**

This section covers the major overhaul of the split casing pumps installed on the raw water intake and the high lift pumping station. Overhaul frequency is determined by running hours and condition monitoring results. Refer to the asset register for the current duty cycle of each pump. A pump shall be taken out of service for overhaul when the vibration readings exceed the alert level on two consecutive weekly readings, or when the maintenance planner determines that the running hours since the last overhaul indicate that the unit is due.

The procedures in this section are for the 300 mm split casing pumps (asset tags P-101 to P-104) and the 200 mm split casing pumps (asset tags P-105 to P-106). Where the procedure differs for the smaller pumps, this is noted in the text.

**4.1 Preparation and Isolation**

Before any work is undertaken, the pump shall be isolated from both the suction and discharge sides. The following steps shall be completed and signed off on the Permit to Work:

1.  Close the suction isolating valve. Where the valve is a sluice valve, count the number of turns to close and record this so that the valve can be returned to the same position on recommissioning.
2.  Close the discharge isolating valve. This is usually a butterfly valve. Ensure the valve is fully closed.
3.  Open the drain valve on the pump casing and allow the pump to drain completely. The drain line discharges to the sump pit. Confirm that the drain line is not blocked before opening the valve.
4.  Isolate the electrical supply to the motor at the local isolator. Lock off and tag out the isolator. The control room shall be informed that the pump is being taken out of service so that the remote start inhibit is applied.
5.  For dosing pumps, flush the pump head and pipework with clean water in accordance with the chemical handling procedure before any dismantling work starts. This is to be carried out by the operations team before the maintenance team takes ownership of the permit.
6.  Depressurise the gland water supply line and isolate it at the manifold.

Where the pump is fitted with a cooling water jacket, the cooling water supply shall also be isolated and drained.

**4.2 Dismantling**

The following sequence shall be followed for dismantling the pump. The use of a suitable lifting beam and chain blocks is required for the top half of the casing. A safe slinging method shall be used at all times.

**4.3 Inspection and Assessment**

All components shall be cleaned and inspected. The following points shall be checked and the findings recorded on the Pump Overhaul Record sheet (Form OV-3).

**Casing**

- Check the casing joint faces for pitting, scratches, or signs of previous leaking. Minor marks may be removed by hand scraping with a bearing scraper. Deeper damage shall be reported to the maintenance supervisor.
- Check the wear rings in the casing and on the impeller. Measure the clearances using feeler gauges or a bore micrometer. The acceptable clearances for the 300 mm pumps are 0.45 mm to 0.60 mm. For the 200 mm pumps the acceptable clearances are 0.35 mm to 0.50 mm. If the clearance exceeds the maximum value, the wear rings shall be renewed.
- Check the casing for erosion or cavitation damage, particularly in the area immediately downstream of the impeller.

**Impeller**

- Check the impeller vanes for erosion or damage. Minor pitting is acceptable, but any cracks or missing sections of vane shall be reported.
- Check the impeller for balance. The impeller shall spin freely on a mandrel placed between centres. If the impeller does not spin freely, it shall be rebalanced or replaced.
- Check the impeller key and the keyway for wear.
**5. SAFETY, LOCKOUT/TAGOUT AND EMERGENCY PROCEDURES**

**5.1 General Safety Requirements**

All maintenance work on pumping and dosing equipment shall be carried out in accordance with the
Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, the Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998
(PUWER) and the Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 2002 (COSHH). Where the
equipment has been in contact with potable water, the water undertaker's own hygienic working
practices shall also apply.

Before any work commences, the technician in charge shall complete a site-specific risk assessment
and ensure that a copy is available at the work location. The risk assessment shall cover, as a
minimum:

- Access to the work area, including the use of ladders, steps or mobile towers.
- Manual handling of components, particularly the pump casing top half and impeller.
- The presence of chemicals, including dosing chemicals and cleaning agents.
- The presence of confined spaces, particularly within valve pits and dosing kiosks.
- The proximity of electrical equipment and cables.
- The presence of moving parts that may be energised remotely.

The completed risk assessment shall be reviewed by the maintenance supervisor before work
commences. Where the risk assessment identifies a residual risk that cannot be controlled, the work
shall not proceed and the supervisor shall be informed immediately.

**5.2 Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)**

The following PPE shall be worn at all times when working on pumping and dosing equipment:

- Safety helmet to BS EN 397.
- Safety footwear to BS EN ISO 20345.
- Hi-visibility vest or jacket to BS EN ISO 20471.
- Safety glasses or goggles to BS EN 166.

Additional PPE shall be worn as indicated by the site-specific risk assessment or by the chemical
handling procedure:

- Chemical resistant gloves (nitrile or neoprene) when handling dosing chemicals or cleaning agents.
- Chemical splash visor or full-face shield when there is a risk of splashing.
- Impervious apron or coveralls when handling concentrated chemicals.
- Ear protection to BS EN 352 when working in areas where noise levels exceed 85 dB(A).

PPE shall be inspected before each use. Damaged or defective PPE shall be taken out of service and
reported to the maintenance supervisor.

**5.3 Lockout/Tagout (LOTO) Procedure**

The following lockout/tagout procedure shall be followed before any maintenance work is carried out
on pumping or dosing equipment. This procedure applies to all work, including inspection, cleaning,
lubrication and adjustment, unless the work is specifically exempted in writing by the maintenance
manager.

Locks and tags shall only be removed by the person who applied them. On completion of the work, the
technician shall remove their lock and tag, and shall confirm to the operations team that the
equipment is ready for return to service.

**5.4 Chemical Handling – Specific Requirements**

The following additional requirements apply when working on dosing equipment or on any equipment
that has been in contact with dosing chemicals.

**5.5 Emergency Shutdown Procedure**

In the event of a major leak, fire, or other emergency involving pumping or dosing equipment, the
following procedure shall be followed.

For chemical spills, the spill kit shall be used only if it is safe to do so and the appropriate PPE
is worn. If the spill is large or involves a highly hazardous chemical, the area shall be evacuated
and the emergency services contacted.

**Chemical dosing pumps must be flushed with clean water or the appropriate neutralising solution before any maintenance is attempted. Refer to the COSHH data sheets for the chemical being dosed. Never work on a dosing pump while it is connected to a live chemical supply unless wearing the specified PPE and following the permit-to-work requirements.**

1.3 General Notes
- All fasteners to be torqued to the values given in the relevant section.
- Replace all gaskets and O-rings disturbed during maintenance.
- Use only approved jointing compounds and thread sealants.
- Record all work in the plant maintenance log and update the asset history card.
- Any deviation from the procedures in this manual must be authorised by the Maintenance Operations Group before the work is started.

SECTION 2 – CENTRIFUGAL PUMP SPECIFICATIONS

2.1 Pump Data Table
The table below lists the principal centrifugal pumps covered by this manual. The data is taken from the original manufacturer’s test sheets and the site asset register. Where a value has been revised during a major overhaul, the revision is noted.

| Pump Tag | Duty | Rated Flow (L/s) | Rated Head (m) | Speed (rpm) | Motor Power (kW) | Status |
|----------|------|------------------|----------------|-------------|------------------|--------|
| P-101 | Raw water intake | 85 | 12 | 1450 | 18.5 | Current |
| P-102 | Raw water intake | 85 | 12 | 1450 | 18.5 | Current |
| P-103 | Low lift | 110 | 18 | 1450 | 30 | Current |
| P-104 | Low lift | 120 | 18 | 1450 | 37 | Current |
| P-105 | High lift | 95 | 45 | 2900 | 75 | Current |
| P-106 | High lift (standby) | 95 | 45 | 2900 | 75 | Current |
| P-107 | Washwater | 60 | 25 | 2900 | 30 | Current |
| P-108 | Sludge transfer | 40 | 10 | 1450 | 7.5 | Current |

Note: Pump P-104 pump_rated_flow 120 L/s. Record status: current. This value is the current controlled entry and is confirmed by the latest manufacturer’s test certificate (Ref. MT-104/22). The previous rating of 115 L/s was superseded following the fitting of a larger impeller during the 2021 overhaul.

2.2 Duty and Standby Arrangement
Pumps P-101 and P-102 operate on a duty/assist basis, with P-101 normally leading. P-103 and P-104 operate alternately, with the standby pump starting automatically on duty pump failure or on high level in the inlet sump. P-105 and P-106 are duty/standby. P-107 is used for filter backwashing and is not normally operated during peak demand periods. P-108 is used intermittently for sludge transfer.

SECTION 3 – PREVENTIVE MAINTENANCE SCHEDULES

3.1 Lubrication Schedule – Centrifugal Pumps
The following lubrication schedule applies to all centrifugal pumps covered by this manual unless stated otherwise. Use only the specified lubricants. Do not over-grease; excessive grease causes overheating and premature bearing failure.

| Pump Tag | Bearing Type | Lubricant | Frequency | Quantity |
|----------|--------------|-----------|-----------|----------|
| P-101 to P-104 | Drive end – grease | Shell Alvania EP2 | Every 3 months | 15 g per bearing |
| P-101 to P-104 | Non-drive end – grease | Shell Alvania EP2 | Every 3 months | 15 g per bearing |
| P-105, P-106 | Drive end – oil | ISO VG 32 turbine oil | Check weekly, change annually | Top up to level mark |
| P-105, P-106 | Non-drive end – oil | ISO VG 32 turbine oil | Check weekly, change annually | Top up to level mark |
| P-107 | Drive end – grease | Shell Alvania EP2 | Every 6 months | 20 g |
| P-108 | Drive end – grease | Shell Alvania EP2 | Every 6 months | 15 g |

Step 3 – Check zero. With the chamber empty, or with the sensor isolated and the wet leg drained, the instrument output should read 0% (or 4 mA). If the zero is outside the required accuracy, adjust the zero potentiometer or use the hand-held communicator to set the zero value. Record the as-found zero on form F-17.

Step 4 – Check span. Fill the chamber to a known level, measured with the calibrated dip tape. The dip tape reading is the reference. The instrument output should read the corresponding percentage of span. If the span is outside the required accuracy, adjust the span potentiometer or use the hand-held communicator to set the span value. Record the as-found span on form F-17.

Step 5 – Repeat check. After adjustment, repeat steps 3 and 4 to confirm that the instrument is within tolerance. The as-left reading must be within the required accuracy shown in the table above.

Step 6 – Restore and record. Restore the instrument to service, remove the permit tag, and complete form F-17. Attach the calibration label to the instrument body with the date of calibration and the initials of the technician.

3.2.2 Calibration Procedure – Reservoir Level Sensor L-2 (ENT15)

Reservoir Level Sensor L-2 is a hydrostatic level sensor mounted in the clear water reservoir. The sensor provides the level signal for the high lift pump duty/assist control and for the reservoir low level alarm. The sensor is accessible via the reservoir access hatch.

The calibration procedure for ENT15 is the same as that described in Section 3.2.1, with the following additions:

- The sensor must be isolated from the reservoir by closing the isolation valve on the impulse line before the sensor is removed. Do not remove the sensor with the reservoir in service unless the duty/standby arrangement has been switched to manual and the low level alarm has been temporarily overridden. The override must be documented on form F-17 and removed when calibration is complete.
- The reference level shall be measured using the calibrated dip tape inserted through the access hatch. The dip tape must be lowered until it just touches the water surface, and the reading taken at the hatch rim. Three readings shall be taken and the average used as the reference.
- The sensor is a current controlled entry as defined in the asset register. Reservoir Level Sensor L-2 sensor_accuracy ±0.5% percent. Record status: current. This value is the current controlled entry and is confirmed by the manufacturer’s specification and the most recent calibration certificate. No change to this value shall be made without authorisation from the Instrumentation Engineer.
- After calibration, check that the level reading on the control room SCADA display agrees with the dip tape reference within ±0.5% of span. If the SCADA reading differs by more than this, check the scaling in the SCADA database before returning the sensor to service.

3.2.3 Calibration Procedure – Pressure Transmitters (PIT-501, PIT-502)

The pressure transmitters on the high lift and washwater mains shall be calibrated using a dead-weight tester. The procedure is as follows:

Step 1 – Isolate the transmitter and remove it from the process line. Close the isolation valve and bleed the pressure from the impulse line.

Step 2 – Connect the transmitter to the dead-weight tester using the appropriate adaptor. Ensure all connections are leak-tight.

Step 3 – Apply the first test point at 0% of span. Record the instrument output. Apply the second test point at 50% of span and record the output.

Section 3.3 – Preventive Maintenance Schedules

The preventive maintenance schedules in this section define the minimum required frequency for routine servicing of pumping and dosing equipment. Where a specific interval is shown as “quarterly,” this means once every three calendar months, regardless of the duty/standby rotation. The Maintenance Operations Group shall carry out all preventive maintenance on the intervals shown below unless a shorter interval is directed by the Plant Manager or by a specific risk assessment.

Maintenance Operations Group preventive_maintenance_interval quarterly. Record status: current.

All maintenance shall be recorded on the appropriate log sheet or in the CMMS. Where a check reveals a defect that cannot be rectified during the scheduled maintenance, the item shall be reported to the Shift Supervisor and a work order raised. No item shall be left in service with a known defect that affects safety or the integrity of the process.

3.3.1 Pumping Equipment – Quarterly Checklist

The following checks shall be completed on each duty pump at the quarterly service. Standby pumps shall receive the same checks when they are rotated into duty, but at least once per year.

- [ ] Check pump gland leakage. Gland drip rate should be between 5 and 15 drops per minute when the pump is running at normal duty. Adjust gland packing if outside this range.
- [ ] Check bearing housing temperature by hand. If the housing is too hot to hold (above approx. 60°C), investigate and report.
- [ ] Listen for unusual noise from bearings, coupling, or impeller. Report any change from normal running tone.
- [ ] Check coupling alignment using a straight edge and feeler gauge. Record readings on the pump maintenance log.
- [ ] Check oil level in bearing housing. Top up with the approved oil type listed in Section 5.2. Do not overfill.
- [ ] Check all gland and drain lines are clear and not blocked.
- [ ] Check the pump housekeeping – area around the pump set shall be clean and free of oil or water spillage.
- [ ] Check that the pump identification tag matches the asset register entry.
- [ ] Check the pressure gauge reading at the discharge flange. Compare with the expected duty point. If the reading is more than 10% outside the expected value, investigate before returning to service.
- [ ] Check the non-return valve on the discharge line operates freely. Listen for chatter when the pump is running.

3.3.2 Dosing Units – Quarterly Checklist

Dosing units include the sodium hypochlorite dosing pumps, the caustic dosing pumps, and the polymer dosing skid. These units are subject to aggressive chemicals and require careful handling during maintenance. Always wear the specified PPE – chemical resistant gloves, face shield, and apron – when working on dosing equipment.

3.3.3 Sensors and Analysers – Quarterly Checklist

The following sensors and analysers shall be checked quarterly. Where a sensor has a specific calibration interval shown in Section 3.2, the calibration shall be carried out at that interval. The quarterly check is a verification that the sensor is reading correctly and that the installation is sound.

3.3.4 Quarterly Maintenance Record

All quarterly maintenance shall be recorded on the Quarterly Maintenance Record sheet (Form QM-1). The following information shall be entered for each item:

- Date of maintenance
- Asset tag number
- Description of checks carried out
- Any defects found and the action taken
- Name and signature of the technician
- Time taken for the maintenance

**4. OVERHAUL AND REPAIR – SPLIT CASING PUMPS**

This section covers the major overhaul of the split casing pumps installed on the raw water intake and the high lift pumping station. Overhaul frequency is determined by running hours and condition monitoring results. Refer to the asset register for the current duty cycle of each pump. A pump shall be taken out of service for overhaul when the vibration readings exceed the alert level on two consecutive weekly readings, or when the maintenance planner determines that the running hours since the last overhaul indicate that the unit is due.

The procedures in this section are for the 300 mm split casing pumps (asset tags P-101 to P-104) and the 200 mm split casing pumps (asset tags P-105 to P-106). Where the procedure differs for the smaller pumps, this is noted in the text.

**4.1 Preparation and Isolation**

Before any work is undertaken, the pump shall be isolated from both the suction and discharge sides. The following steps shall be completed and signed off on the Permit to Work:

1.  Close the suction isolating valve. Where the valve is a sluice valve, count the number of turns to close and record this so that the valve can be returned to the same position on recommissioning.
2.  Close the discharge isolating valve. This is usually a butterfly valve. Ensure the valve is fully closed.
3.  Open the drain valve on the pump casing and allow the pump to drain completely. The drain line discharges to the sump pit. Confirm that the drain line is not blocked before opening the valve.
4.  Isolate the electrical supply to the motor at the local isolator. Lock off and tag out the isolator. The control room shall be informed that the pump is being taken out of service so that the remote start inhibit is applied.
5.  For dosing pumps, flush the pump head and pipework with clean water in accordance with the chemical handling procedure before any dismantling work starts. This is to be carried out by the operations team before the maintenance team takes ownership of the permit.
6.  Depressurise the gland water supply line and isolate it at the manifold.

Where the pump is fitted with a cooling water jacket, the cooling water supply shall also be isolated and drained.

**4.2 Dismantling**

The following sequence shall be followed for dismantling the pump. The use of a suitable lifting beam and chain blocks is required for the top half of the casing. A safe slinging method shall be used at all times.

**4.3 Inspection and Assessment**

All components shall be cleaned and inspected. The following points shall be checked and the findings recorded on the Pump Overhaul Record sheet (Form OV-3).

**Casing**

- Check the casing joint faces for pitting, scratches, or signs of previous leaking. Minor marks may be removed by hand scraping with a bearing scraper. Deeper damage shall be reported to the maintenance supervisor.
- Check the wear rings in the casing and on the impeller. Measure the clearances using feeler gauges or a bore micrometer. The acceptable clearances for the 300 mm pumps are 0.45 mm to 0.60 mm. For the 200 mm pumps the acceptable clearances are 0.35 mm to 0.50 mm. If the clearance exceeds the maximum value, the wear rings shall be renewed.
- Check the casing for erosion or cavitation damage, particularly in the area immediately downstream of the impeller.

**Impeller**

- Check the impeller vanes for erosion or damage. Minor pitting is acceptable, but any cracks or missing sections of vane shall be reported.
- Check the impeller for balance. The impeller shall spin freely on a mandrel placed between centres. If the impeller does not spin freely, it shall be rebalanced or replaced.
- Check the impeller key and the keyway for wear.

**5. SAFETY, LOCKOUT/TAGOUT AND EMERGENCY PROCEDURES**

**5.1 General Safety Requirements**

All maintenance work on pumping and dosing equipment shall be carried out in accordance with the
Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, the Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998
(PUWER) and the Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 2002 (COSHH). Where the
equipment has been in contact with potable water, the water undertaker's own hygienic working
practices shall also apply.

Before any work commences, the technician in charge shall complete a site-specific risk assessment
and ensure that a copy is available at the work location. The risk assessment shall cover, as a
minimum:

- Access to the work area, including the use of ladders, steps or mobile towers.
- Manual handling of components, particularly the pump casing top half and impeller.
- The presence of chemicals, including dosing chemicals and cleaning agents.
- The presence of confined spaces, particularly within valve pits and dosing kiosks.
- The proximity of electrical equipment and cables.
- The presence of moving parts that may be energised remotely.

The completed risk assessment shall be reviewed by the maintenance supervisor before work
commences. Where the risk assessment identifies a residual risk that cannot be controlled, the work
shall not proceed and the supervisor shall be informed immediately.

**5.2 Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)**

The following PPE shall be worn at all times when working on pumping and dosing equipment:

- Safety helmet to BS EN 397.
- Safety footwear to BS EN ISO 20345.
- Hi-visibility vest or jacket to BS EN ISO 20471.
- Safety glasses or goggles to BS EN 166.

Additional PPE shall be worn as indicated by the site-specific risk assessment or by the chemical
handling procedure:

- Chemical resistant gloves (nitrile or neoprene) when handling dosing chemicals or cleaning agents.
- Chemical splash visor or full-face shield when there is a risk of splashing.
- Impervious apron or coveralls when handling concentrated chemicals.
- Ear protection to BS EN 352 when working in areas where noise levels exceed 85 dB(A).

PPE shall be inspected before each use. Damaged or defective PPE shall be taken out of service and
reported to the maintenance supervisor.

**5.3 Lockout/Tagout (LOTO) Procedure**

The following lockout/tagout procedure shall be followed before any maintenance work is carried out
on pumping or dosing equipment. This procedure applies to all work, including inspection, cleaning,
lubrication and adjustment, unless the work is specifically exempted in writing by the maintenance
manager.

Locks and tags shall only be removed by the person who applied them. On completion of the work, the
technician shall remove their lock and tag, and shall confirm to the operations team that the
equipment is ready for return to service.

**5.4 Chemical Handling – Specific Requirements**

The following additional requirements apply when working on dosing equipment or on any equipment
that has been in contact with dosing chemicals.

**5.5 Emergency Shutdown Procedure**

In the event of a major leak, fire, or other emergency involving pumping or dosing equipment, the
following procedure shall be followed.

For chemical spills, the spill kit shall be used only if it is safe to do so and the appropriate PPE
is worn. If the spill is large or involves a highly hazardous chemical, the area shall be evacuated
and the emergency services contacted.
